comments.author: @seikojin
comments.text: Much like I have been saying for a little bit now: AI right now is token prediction. It takes a lot of pre-conditioning statement, using valuable tokens per session, to prepare these LLM's to do a specific task. And the more tokens used = the more confusing each prediction becomes, making the LLM produce incorrect responses, or veering from the path needed. Maybe, instead of trying to head toward general intelligence, we condition agents, pretrained for specific contexts, and then use them in an concert of agents managed by the user/orchestration agent. All it would be doing is predicting, based on input tokens, what agents would have the correct training to specific context.

AI systems will be the new supercomputer/mainframe which everyone has work for, but have a limited amount available - often determined by leadership.  HIgh interactivity tasks might get working hours access, where large bulk processes could be done after-hours using cheaper electricity. comments.text:
The real danger isn’t AI itself, it’s how it’s being used to expand the power of the existing ruling class. The same global elite, the top bankers, corporations, and wealth hoarders are now positioning themselves to control the future through AI. They talk about "innovation" and "efficiency," but their goal is clear: automate everything, eliminate resistance, and tighten control.

But we don’t have to accept that future. We can flip the script and build a system that works for everyone, not just the 1%. Imagine a world where AI frees us from meaningless labor, not to make billionaires richer, but to give everyone a life of dignity and purpose. Where basic needs are guaranteed.

Where land and resources are shared and managed collectively, not privately owned for profit or control. In this system, private property as a tool of exploitation is abolished, no one has the right to hoard land, water, or infrastructure that all of humanity depends on. But at the same time, personal property is fully respected and guaranteed. Your home, your clothes, your tools, your space—these are yours, not because of wealth or ownership titles, but because every human being deserves security, dignity, and autonomy.

Where decisions are made directly by the people, with guidance from those who truly understand and care, not from so-called “experts” manufactured by the system.


That’s what Open Direct Competent Democracy (ODCD) and the Natural Law Economy (NLE) aim to create: a world where technology serves humanity and nature, not the other way around.

We’re not heading toward dystopia because of AI, we’re heading there because we’ve let the same old powers write the rules. But that can change. It must change.

Hopelessness is a trap they want us to fall into. But we are not helpless. We can still choose a different path together.

comments.author: @gavinx3
comments.text:
Although I agree with the sentiment that "AI orchestrator" may be a limited-time position, I wonder where the intersection is between human will and AI will. At present, the AI doesn't have a will of its own. A human still has to tell it a task to do. AI may be able to create and manage a whole company by itself, but without a human to tell it what company to create, will it want to? Currently AI can create music, but it's not autonomously and endlessly creating its own albums. When will this change? Will AI ever have a will of its own? If never, humans will be at the top of the loop. If they eventually have super intelligence, and the will to command it, then we will likely be passengers in a new type of society— living passively as a vestigial organ of a greater being. 

Will or not, this says nothing about the finite resources that will have to be managed without humans simply sending another prompt, and demanding their will be autonomously executed by robotic and agentic swarms. 

This leads to an age-old philosophical question put into modern terms: are we cooked?

comments.author: @CodyLandry
comments.text:
I disagree.  Yes, being able to orchestrate well will be important, but more importantly will be the ability to validate.  While it will still be a while before AI can do 'everything', it will be much longer before we trust that AI does 'everything' CORRECTLY.  

Its similar to self driving cars.  Self driving cars have come a long way and in some cases are truly autonomous, yet we still have steering wheels and require drivers to watch the road and be ready to take over.  Even after self driving cars achieve 100% success rate, it will be years before we trust them enough to start removing steering wheels and letting people take naps on the freeway.

Its no different with AI coding.  The danger is still too great that AI will create major security vulnerabilities, leaks or breaking changes.  

The great thing is that the skills we use today to build things by hand are the same ones we use to validate AI's output now and for the foreseeable future.
